WMT.rationale: Walmart is a fundamentally sound business with a durable franchise, but the stock is priced at historical extremes that leave no margin of safety. Trailing P/E of 54.5x (+67% YoY expansion) and P/B of 11.8x are at the ceiling of their 365-day ranges, while the 1.8% earnings yield sits 254bp below the 10-year Treasury yield of 4.34%. The multiple has expanded far faster than the business: EPS grew +35.1% YoY while the PE expanded +67%, meaning the ~43% price appreciation is predominantly a multiple story. Sequentially, earnings deteriorated—EPS fell -12.5% QoQ and operating cash flow dropped -29.7% QoQ—contradicting the accelerating-growth narrative the valuation demands. Operating margin compressed from ~4.1% to ~3.7% QoQ despite revenue growth, and oil at $99/bbl (+64% over the lookback window) is a direct cost headwind for a logistics-intensive retailer with only 2.8% net margins. Grocery market share is eroding (20.4% → 19.9% over two years). Management's FY2027 EPS guidance of $2.75–$2.85 came in below the $2.96 consensus, signaling the company itself does not expect to meet the growth trajectory the market has priced in. The Henry Fund's $83 DCF target underscores the intrinsic-value disconnect. All three pillars align negatively: deteriorating sequential fundamentals, extreme valuation vs. own history, and a near-term downside catalyst (tariff-driven margin pressure and below-consensus guidance).
